name: The Cave Mouth
description: The threshold between worlds. Behind you: the last light, birdsong, warm air. Ahead: darkness that breathes cold. The transition happens in twenty feet — daylight to memory, wind to stillness, the complex surface world to the cave's single ancient mineral chord.

layers.note: fading as you face inward — the forest is letting go
each drop is 0.05 mL hitting stone from 2m — sharp plink with a 0.8s reverb tail
infrasound you feel more than hear — the cave breathing out through you

surface_textures: moss-covered rock at the entrance — soft, wet, yielding under fingers, living on dead stone
bare limestone deeper in — cold, slick with condensation, rougher than the weathered exterior
gravel underfoot at the threshold — loose, crunching, river-rounded stones mixed with angular fragments
fern fronds brushing your arms at the entrance — wet, cool, feathered edges
touch.air_feel: The cave breathes outward — a constant gentle exhalation of 13°C air against your face, damp enough to feel on your lips. It smells of deep earth and mineral patience. Behind you, the outside air is warmer, drier, alive with pollen and insect wing-beats. You're standing in the breath of something much older than you.
touch.thermal_notes: A gradient: warm back, cold face. The cave's exhalation creates a clean thermal boundary you can map with your skin. Step forward and the temperature drops 2°C in a meter. The humidity climbs. Your body notices the transition as a single event — like stepping into water, but with air.
key_tactile_moments: The first touch of cold air on your face — the cave introducing itself
Reaching out to the wall and finding it wet — not dripping, just perpetually damp, the stone sweating
The gravel shifting under your weight — the last unstable ground before the cave floor smooths to bedrock

cross_sensory_bridges: The light and the sound die together — as daylight fades, the birdsong fades with it, until both are gone and you're in a world that runs on different senses entirely.
The cave's breath carries its smell — the outward wind is how you know what's inside before you see it. Mineral water, wet stone, deep earth. The cave tells you what it is through the air it exhales.
Moss grows exactly where the light still reaches. The boundary between green and bare stone is the boundary between two worlds. Your hand finds it before your eyes do.
prose:
The cave mouth is a sentence that starts in sunlight and ends in the dark.

You stand at the entrance — an irregular arch of limestone, wider than it is tall, draped in ferns and moss that soften its edges into something almost biological. Light falls inward for perhaps twenty feet before the rock swallows it. The air here moves outward, a steady cool exhalation that smells of wet stone and centuries. It pushes against your face and chest with the gentleness of something that has been breathing for longer than your species has existed.

The threshold is visible in every sense. Light dies. Sound changes — the open-air acoustic of birds and wind compresses into the tight, reflective clarity of enclosed stone. The temperature drops. The humidity rises until the air feels thick enough to touch. The smell shifts from the complex organic soup of the surface — leaf litter, pollen, warm earth — to the cave's single mineral note: calcium carbonate dissolved in water, the smell of geology happening in real time.

Behind you, the world you know. Ahead, a darkness that isn't empty — it's full of dripping water, echoing silence, and the patient work of stone. The ferns at the entrance are the last green thing. The moss is the last soft thing. After this, everything is rock.

You can still feel the sun on your back.

positions.name: the threshold
positions.prose: You stand exactly where the light gives up. One step back and you're in dappled forest. One step forward and you need a lamp. The air moves around you in two directions — warm at your back, cold on your face — and your body is the boundary between them.
positions.cross_sensory: The temperature gradient maps perfectly onto the light gradient — warm where it's bright, cold where it's dark. Your skin and your eyes are telling you the same story.
positions.touch_notes: The ground transitions here: soft forest soil behind you, loose gravel at your feet, smooth bedrock ahead. Three surfaces in five steps.

light.note: The light gradient covers three orders of magnitude in twenty feet. Your pupils dilate from 2mm to 7mm crossing the threshold — a 12x increase in light gathering. It's not enough.

impossible_detail: The moss boundary is at exactly 15 lux — the minimum photosynthetically active radiation for bryophytes. Below that line, nothing photosynthetic survives. You can find the boundary with your hand: where moss ends and bare stone begins, that's where the cave starts and the sun gives up.
